summary: 60-min technical deep dive focused on throughput tuning for BrightScale's latency-sensitive chat pipeline. Covered continuous batching, scheduler knobs, max_num_seqs, token limits, KV cache warmup, and quantization impacts. Agreed next steps: Redwood sends config examples and SE-guidance; BrightScale runs a sustained benchmark and shares logs; follow-up scheduled to iterate on quantization and scheduler settings.
transcript:
00:00:00 Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. quick roll call, um Liam from Redwood will be joining for the deep dive.
00:00:12 Alex Kim: Alex here, Priya and Daniel on from BrightScale. we have a heavy customers-facing chat endpoint that spikes at peak and we want to push more throughput without breaking latency SLOs.
00:00:30 Liam O'Rourke: Cool. quick agenda: continuous batching overview, scheduler knobs (max_num_seqs, preempt policies), token limits, KV cache warmup, quantization tradeoffs, then sizing recommendations for VPC/on-prem.
00:00:47 Daniel Park: Sounds good, we mostly care about 95th latency under 300ms for short completions and cost per 1M tokens.
00:01:05 Maya Chen: Great, note we'll likely recommend a mix: smaller sequence batching for low-latency endpoints + burst capacity for spikes.
00:01:22 Priya Rao: Quick context: we're using our own VPC deployment, running Redwood Dedicate (sic) on G4-like nodes, currently 8 GPUs with mixed workloads. average seq len is 16 tokens, tail events hit 256 tokens.
00:01:45 Liam O'Rourke: Okay, that helps. first, continuous batching — our runtime maintains an open batch window and fills it with incoming requests up to max_num_seqs or token budget. key knobs: max_num_seqs, max_total_tokens_per_batch, and commit_timeout.
00:02:10 Liam O'Rourke: if you set max_num_seqs too high you get great throughput but the first-token latency suffers because requests wait to fill the batch. keep it lower for latency-critical routes.
00:02:30 Alex Kim: our current max_num_seqs is 64, seems like it helps throughput but we see 95th go beyond 400ms during busy minutes.
00:02:44 Liam O'Rourke: 64 is high for short sequences. given avg 16 tokens, and model kv cache behavior, we usually suggest starting with 8-16 for chat flows and rely on micro-bursts to scale via burst pools.
00:03:05 Daniel Park: micro-bursts? how does Redwood handle burst capacity in Dedicated/VPC?
00:03:15 Maya Chen: we provide configurable burst capacity and autoscaling policies on Dedicated; for VPC you can set a local burst pool or enable cross-region fallback. but, on-prem customers need to size nodes for expected peak or accept slightly degraded tail latency.
00:03:40 Priya Rao: For VPC we want to avoid spinning new nodes during spikes due to startup time. does continuous batching help with spikes without adding nodes?
00:03:55 Liam O'Rourke: yes and no. continuous batching smooths short spikes by packing more sequences into batches, but only up to existing GPU capacity. if spikes exceed peak throughput capacity then you need burst nodes or fallback to cheaper model variants.
00:04:15 Alex Kim: ok got it. can you walk through an example of how max_num_seqs and token limits interact?
00:04:25 Liam O'Rourke: sure. suppose max_num_seqs=16 and max_total_tokens_per_batch=2048. if you get 16 requests each asking for 64 tokens, that's 1024 total tokens — fine. but if you had heavier requests hitting tail 256 tokens, you might hit the token cap first and batch smaller number of sequences. order matters: runtime fills by arrival and stops when either cap hits.
00:04:55 Priya Rao: so if token limits are reached we get smaller batch size which can increase per-token overhead?
00:05:05 Liam O'Rourke: Exactly — smaller batch sizes reduce kernel parallelism efficiency. tradeoff between latency and throughput.
00:05:18 Daniel Park: What's the sweet spot for our profile (avg 16, tail 256)?
00:05:26 Liam O'Rourke: start with max_num_seqs=12, max_total_tokens_per_batch=4096, commit_timeout=12ms. that aims to keep first-token latency low while allowing token-heavy tails to still utilize batching.
00:05:44 Alex Kim: commit_timeout 12ms — is that safe? we saw some jitter at <10ms on our infra.
00:05:52 Liam O'Rourke: if your infra is jittery, bump to 20-25ms; lower timeouts reduce wait but cause more smaller batches. we can provide a chart showing expected throughput vs 95th latency at different timeout values.
00:06:10 Maya Chen: we'll attach that chart. next, KV cache warmup — for chat where you do multi-turn, warm KV caches by pinning frequent prefixes or using prefix caching.
00:06:23 Priya Rao: currently we drop KV between requests since we’re multi-tenant and worried about memory. any recommendations?
00:06:33 Liam O'Rourke: two options: tenant-local KV cache (recommended) or shared compressed cache. tenant-local gives best perf; if memory is constrained, set aggressive eviction for cold tenants and pin hot prefixes. also quantization affects KV memory footprint.
00:06:52 Alex Kim: quantization — we tried 4-bit and saw small quality regressions but huge throughput gains. what's Redwood's guidance?
00:07:02 Liam O'Rourke: 4-bit integer quantization (Q4) often gives 2x throughput on transformer kernels, but some tasks see quality drop. Redwood Optimize can run eval sets on your prompt/response pairs to estimate regression. we usually recommend model-specific profiles: Q4 for stateless or short-chat prompts, Q8 or FP16 for long-form generation.
00:07:27 Daniel Park: does quantization change KV behavior?
00:07:32 Liam O'Rourke: yes — KV cache stored with quantized keys/values reduces memory and memory bandwidth pressure, so you get better batching efficiency for the same hardware. but keep an eye on end-to-end quality.
00:07:46 Priya Rao: any presets for our G4-like nodes?
00:07:50 Liam O'Rourke: We'll share a preset that sets: max_num_seqs:12, max_total_tokens:4096, commit_timeout:20ms, batch_scheduler: latency_pref, quant_profile: Q4-mixed with spill to Q8 for long sequences.
00:08:08 Alex Kim: nice. you mentioned batch_scheduler: latency_pref — what other scheduler modes exist?
00:08:15 Liam O'Rourke: two common modes: latency_pref (prioritizes first-token latency, preempts batches to serve waiting low-latency reqs) and throughput_pref (maximizes GPU utilization, larger batches, higher tail latency). we also have an adaptive mode which tries to balance using runtime heuristics.
00:08:37 Maya Chen: for BrightScale’s 95th <300ms target, start latency_pref then measure and relax to adaptive if you need more throughput.
00:08:49 Daniel Park: How do we measure impact? what metrics do you recommend?
00:08:55 Liam O'Rourke: collect per-route first-token-latency, per-token-latency, batch-size distribution, GPU util, and KV hit-rate. Redwood Console shows token-level cost broken down by model and route and will plot batch-size histograms.
00:09:12 Priya Rao: do you have an example of expected GPU util vs throughput for our config?
00:09:18 Liam O'Rourke: yes, we'll attach a matrix. rough numbers: with max_num_seqs=12 and Q4, expect ~70% GPU util at steady state for your load; throughput_pref could push to 90% but may break 95th latency.
00:09:36 Alex Kim: about warmup — how long does KV heating take?
00:09:40 Liam O'Rourke: usually a few minutes of steady traffic to stabilize hot prefixes; for large context windows or long histories it can be longer. we recommend starting a short synthetic warmup run that hits top 10 prefixes to prepopulate caches before peak.
00:09:58 Priya Rao: interesting. we can do that. any hooks to pre-warm on deploy?
00:10:05 Liam O'Rourke: yes, Redwood provides a warmup API you can call with representative prompts to populate caches, and the Dedicated control plane can run warmup jobs on rollout.
00:10:18 Daniel Park: on quantization again — will switching to Q4 change memory requirements for batch size planning?
00:10:25 Liam O'Rourke: significantly — Q4 typically halves memory for weights and KV, letting you increase max_total_tokens_per_batch or max_num_seqs. but you still need to measure GPU memory headroom for activation peaks.
00:10:40 Maya Chen: quick break — any compliance or security blockers for VPC?
00:10:47 Alex Kim: we need to ensure audit logs and KMS integration. BrightScale requires HSM for keys and SOC2 level audit trails.
00:10:58 Maya Chen: Redwood Private supports KMS/HSM integrations and per-request audit logs; we'll include our SOC2/ISO docs in follow-up.
00:11:10 Priya Rao: good. now scheduling knobs: you mentioned preempt policies — can you explain?
00:11:16 Liam O'Rourke: preempt policies let high-priority requests interrupt low priority batches to meet latency SLOs. options: soft-preempt (mark and finish current micro-batch quickly), hard-preempt (stop batch immediately), or sandboxed lanes (reserve a small set of sequences per GPU for high-priority traffic).
00:11:37 Alex Kim: sandboxed lanes sounds useful — reserve say 10% capacity?
00:11:42 Liam O'Rourke: yes, typically 5-15% depending on tail sensitivity. sandboxed lanes ensure critical traffic hits low queuing time without complex preemption logic.
00:11:54 Daniel Park: benchmarking — what harness do you recommend?
00:11:58 Liam O'Rourke: Redwood test harness supports sustained open-loop and closed-loop tests. for throughput you'll run open-loop at your target concurrency to measure GPU saturation and tail latencies. we'll share the harness and a sample JMeter script.
00:12:12 Maya Chen: we'll include a sample benchmark plan in the follow-up email.
00:12:18 Alex Kim: earlier you mentioned adaptive scheduler heuristics — how transparent are those? can we force deterministic behavior for debugging?
00:12:25 Liam O'Rourke: yes, adaptive has tunable thresholds; we expose flags: adaptive_window_size, min_batch_fill, and aggressiveness. you can set deterministic modes to lock to latency_pref or throughput_pref for debugging.
00:12:40 Priya Rao: logging — what should we collect from Redwood side if something goes wrong?
00:12:45 Liam O'Rourke: collect per-request headers (route, sequence length), batch metadata (batch id, size, token sum), GPU perf counters (util, mem), and KV hit/miss logs. Redwood support can ingest zipped logs.
00:13:02 Alex Kim: ok we will coordinate access.
00:13:06 Daniel Park: are there any hidden gotchas for mixed workloads? we run embedding jobs during off-peak too.
00:13:12 Liam O'Rourke: mixed workloads can cause head-of-line blocking; recommend separate queues or dedicated pools for embeddings vs chat; embeddings are batch-friendly and should be routed to throughput_pref pools.
00:13:27 Priya Rao: does Redwood Console show cross-route interference metrics?
00:13:31 Liam O'Rourke: yes, per-pool and per-route dashboards show contention and you can set routing policies to isolate workloads.
00:13:40 Maya Chen: time check — 40 minutes in. any other top-level questions before we dive into config examples?
00:13:47 Alex Kim: let's see the config examples then.
00:13:50 Liam O'Rourke: (screen share) config snippet example: 

commit_timeout_ms: 20
max_num_seqs: 12
max_total_tokens_per_batch: 4096
batch_scheduler: latency_pref
preempt_policy: sandboxed_lanes
quant_profile: Q4-mixed

00:14:20 Priya Rao: can you annotate where to change for longer tail sequences?
00:14:24 Liam O'Rourke: for long tails increase max_total_tokens_per_batch to 8192 and bump sandboxed lanes to 10% and consider spill to Q8 when single-request tokens > 512 so kernels don't get memory thrash.
00:14:42 Alex Kim: about spill to Q8 — is it automatic?
00:14:45 Liam O'Rourke: currently it's a configured policy: quant_spill_threshold_tokens: 512 and quant_spill_action: use_Q8. we'll include that in example.
00:14:56 Daniel Park: in our VPC we prefer deterministic policies. is the spill deterministic?
00:15:02 Liam O'Rourke: yes, it's rule-based and deterministic. you can also add a confidence threshold based on eval metrics before enabling spill for a route.
00:15:12 Priya Rao: any note on tokenizer and token counting mismatches that might affect token limits?
00:15:18 Liam O'Rourke: good call — ensure your client-side tokenization matches runtime tokenizer. mismatches lead to unexpected token caps and truncated responses. we saw teams forget to align BPE vs SentencePiece.
00:15:31 Alex Kim: oof. we use a different tokenizer in client microservice — we'll sync to runtime tokenizer.
00:15:36 Maya Chen: action item: Liam to include note and snippet to validate tokenization parity.
00:15:44 Liam O'Rourke: will do. next, sample measurement plan for 1-hour sustained run: ramp to target qps over 5 minutes, sustain for 50 minutes, then cool down. collect histograms at 1s intervals.
00:16:00 Alex Kim: for sustained run, how do we account for KV warmup?
00:16:04 Liam O'Rourke: do a 10min warmup at low concurrency hitting hot prefixes, then ramp to full load; include a second 10min warmup after model cold restart to measure steady-state.
00:16:16 Priya Rao: great. can you talk about per-request QoS headers for routing?
00:16:21 Liam O'Rourke: add headers: x-rd-priority (high/normal), x-rd-expected-tokens, and x-rd-tenant-hint to help runtime route and reserve lanes. we'll share header schema.
00:16:33 Daniel Park: will the headers be visible in logs for debug?
00:16:36 Liam O'Rourke: yes, they are logged if you enable request-logging in the route config. be mindful of PII — Redwood supports redaction rules.
00:16:47 Alex Kim: ok. let's speak about cost tradeoffs — any rule of thumb of cost delta when moving from latency_pref to throughput_pref?
00:16:56 Liam O'Rourke: throughput_pref usually reduces cost per token by 15-40% due to better GPU packing, but increases 95th latency. exact number depends on seq lengths and model; we'll include an example cost model spreadsheet.
00:17:12 Priya Rao: perfect. are there recommended alarms for safe autopruning of quantization changes?
00:17:18 Liam O'Rourke: set quality regression alerts tied to eval prompts (e.g., BLEU/ROUGE or custom metrics) and threshold to rollback. Redwood Optimize can automate that and trigger rollbacks if regressions detected.
00:17:32 Daniel Park: last thing — multi-tenant isolation? we need per-tenant rate limiting and KV isolation.
00:17:38 Liam O'Rourke: isolate via tenant-local caches and per-tenant pool quotas; Redwood Dedicated supports strict RBAC and per-tenant resource reservations.
00:17:50 Maya Chen: wrap up — to recap next steps: Maya sends SOC2/KMS docs; Liam sends scheduler knobs doc + charts + quant profiles + harness; Alex runs 1h benchmark and shares logs; schedule follow-up next week.
00:18:05 Alex Kim: correct. thanks.
00:18:07 Priya Rao: thanks everyone.
00:18:09 Daniel Park: thanks.
00:18:11 Maya Chen: end notes: we'll email the attachments; meeting recording and transcript should be in the shared folder.
